screens.title: STL Iterators and Algorithms
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on two interlocking parts of the STL: iterators and algorithms. Iterators act like generalized, safe pointers that let code traverse containers without knowing how the container stores data. Algorithms are generic functions that operate over iterator-defined ranges, following the common convention of including the first iterator but excluding the second—what we call the range from begin up to, but not including, end. You will learn how iterator categories determine what operations are available, why some algorithms require certain categories, and how lambda functions make algorithms concise and expressive. We'll work through examples with std::vector and std::list, demonstrate common algorithms such as std::sort, std::find, std::for_each, and std::transform, and show the important erase-remove idiom for filtering data. Along the way, you'll see practical pitfalls like iterator invalidation and how to avoid them. By the end of this chapter you will recognize the right iterator category, choose the correct algorithm for a task, and write compact, safe transformations using lambdas. Think about a container you use most often and how these tools will let you process its elements without writing container-specific loops.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › STL Iterators and Algorithms
STL Iterators and Algorithms
A foundation for generic, reusable operations on containers.
Iterators give a uniform way to access elements across containers using begin and end. Algorithms accept iterator ranges and perform tasks like sorting, finding, transforming, and counting. Using lambdas with algorithms keeps code concise and expressive. You will see examples for common tasks and learn safety rules such as iterator invalidation and the erase-remove idiom.
In this lesson
Iterators as smart pointers, iterator categories, algorithms and lambdas.
Coming up
Sort, find, transform, count_if, remove_if, and erase-remove idiom.
Practice
Filter and convert sensor readings with algorithms and lambdas.
Concept map
Iterators → Ranges → Algorithms → Lambdas
Iterators
Generalized pointers from begin() to end().
Algorithms
Generic functions operating on ranges.
Lambdas
Inline predicates and transformations.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to reason about iterators and use them confidently with STL algorithms. First, you will understand iterators as generalized pointers and the importance of the [begin, end) range convention. Second, you will be able to distinguish iterator categories — input, output, forward, bidirectional, and random access — and match them to algorithm requirements. Third, you'll use iterator-based algorithms such as std::sort, std::find, std::for_each, std::transform, std::count_if, and std::remove_if, applying lambda functions as concise predicates or operations. Finally, you'll master safety patterns like the erase-remove idiom and avoid iterator invalidation by re-obtaining iterators after modifying containers. Each objective focuses on both conceptual understanding and practical application so you can write idiomatic and safe STL code. Imagine filtering sensor readings with std::remove_if and transforming the remaining values with std::transform; these are the exact skills you'll practice. A quick verification milestone follows each objective so you can check your competency.

screens.title: What is an iterator?
screens.narratorSegment: An iterator is best understood as a generalized pointer that provides a uniform interface to traverse elements inside any STL container. It lets code use the same stepping and dereference operations across vectors, lists, sets, and other containers despite different underlying layouts. A container offers begin and end: begin returns an iterator to the first element, and end returns a sentinel positioned one past the last element. The half-open range [begin, end) is fundamental: it includes the element pointed to by begin and excludes the sentinel end. This convention simplifies loops and algorithms because an empty range has equal begin and end. A concrete example is iterating a vector with a traditional loop that increases the iterator until it equals end, dereferencing each iterator to access values. A common misconception is treating end as a valid element — dereferencing end is undefined. Another subtle point is that iterators hide container internals so your algorithm doesn't depend on contiguous memory or node structure. Key takeaways: treat iterators like pointers, always use [begin, end) to define ranges, and never dereference end. How might this change the way you write loops when switching from a raw array to an STL container?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Iterators generalize pointers; ranges use [begin, end) so algorithms work uniformly across containers.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › What is an iterator?
Iterator as a generalized pointer
Iterators provide ++ and * operations so algorithms can traverse containers uniformly.
  • • begin() returns first element's iterator; end() is one past the last element.
  • • Ranges are half-open: [begin, end) — common in STL algorithms.
  • • Treat iterators like pointers: do not dereference end(), and compare iterators to test for termination.
Concrete example
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>

std::vector<int> v = {5,2,8};
for (std::vector<int>::iterator it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ++it) {
  std::cout << *it << " ";
}
Key Takeaway

Use [begin, end) consistently. Iterators behave like pointers but are container-aware.

Misconception
End is not an element. Dereferencing end leads to undefined behavior.
Why it matters
Algorithms expect ranges; consistent ranges allow reuse of generic functions across containers.
Try this
Replace an index loop over an array with iterator-based iteration to enforce container independence.

screens.title: Iterator operations — read and write
screens.narratorSegment: Iterators support a small set of operations that depend on their category, but the most fundamental are dereference and increment. Dereferencing an iterator with the star operator gives access to the element; using pre-increment advances the iterator to the next position. With writable iterators you can assign through the dereference to change the container's element. For example, given a vector of integers you can loop using an iterator, multiply each value in place, and the container will be updated. A useful way to think about this is: iterators provide controlled access to elements without exposing container internals. One concrete example: replacing values by assigning *it = newValue inside a loop. A common misconception is treating iterators as indexes; while random access iterators support arithmetic like it + n, many iterators only allow ++ and cannot jump arbitrarily. When writing code, prefer range-based for loops when you only need read access, but use explicit iterators when algorithms require iterator types or when you need fine-grained control over traversal. Closing question: when would you prefer to write through an iterator instead of collecting results in a separate output container?

keyIdea.title: Operations
keyIdea.text: Dereference to read/write; use increment to advance. Only some iterators support arithmetic.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Iterator operations
Read and write via iterators
Use *it to access and ++it to advance. Assignment through *it modifies the element in place.
  • • Read: value = *it
  • • Write: *it = newValue
  • • Move: ++it or it++ (prefer pre-increment for iterators)
Example
for (auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ++it) {
  *it = *it * 2; // modify in place
}
When to use
Use explicit iterators when algorithms expect iterators or when you need to erase or insert at specific positions while iterating.
Common mistake
Assuming you can use arithmetic like it + 3 on every iterator. Only random access iterators support that.
Pro tip
Use range-based for loops for readability when only reading; use iterators when you need the iterator type or to modify in place.
Key Takeaway

Dereference and increment are the core operations; know whether your iterator supports random access before using arithmetic.

screens.title: Iterator categories
screens.narratorSegment: Iterator categories classify what operations an iterator supports and therefore what algorithms can use them. Input iterators allow single-pass reading with ++ and dereference for reading. Output iterators permit writing values once as you advance. Forward iterators can read and write multiple times while moving forward; they are multi-pass. Bidirectional iterators add the ability to move backward with --, which is necessary for containers like std::list. Random access iterators expose arithmetic such as it + n, it[n], and comparison operators so algorithms that jump around, like std::sort, can perform efficiently. A helpful way to remember this is as a capability ladder: each category adds more power. A concrete example: std::vector provides random access iterators, letting std::sort operate on it directly. std::list provides only bidirectional iterators and cannot be sorted with std::sort; instead use list::sort. A common misconception is expecting all containers to support random access operations; this will either fail to compile or be inefficient. When choosing an algorithm, check the minimum iterator category it requires. Which container you pick often determines which algorithms are available to you. Iterator categories means iterator categories add capabilities; match an algorithm's requirement to a container's iterator.. In practical terms, input, output, forward, bidirectional, random access — what each allows. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Iterator categories
Input Iterator
Single-pass read; supports ++ and * for reading.
Use when you only need to consume data once, like reading from a stream.
Output Iterator
Single-pass write; used to send values to an output range.
Often used with std::transform when writing into an output sequence.
Forward Iterator
Multi-pass forward read/write.
More stable than input/output; allows revisiting elements via new iterators.
Bidirectional Iterator
Adds -- for backward traversal.
Example: std::list iterators.
Random Access Iterator
Supports arithmetic, indexing, and comparisons.
Example: std::vector iterators; required by std::sort.
Key Takeaway

Know the iterator category of your container before using algorithms that require higher capabilities.

screens.title: Algorithms and their iterator requirements
screens.narratorSegment: STL algorithms are written generically, but many depend on the iterator category for correctness or performance. For example, std::sort requires random access iterators because it needs to jump to arbitrary positions and compare elements at non-sequential offsets; these operations use iterator arithmetic and indexing. Attempting to pass std::list iterators to std::sort will fail at compile time because std::list provides bidirectional iterators only. In contrast, std::find and std::for_each work with input or forward iterators because they only move forward and examine elements sequentially. The implication is practical: choose container types based on the algorithms you intend to use. If you need frequent random-access sorting and indexing, std::vector is a natural fit. If your data needs stable iterators when inserting and erasing in the middle, std::list offers stability but sacrifices random access. A common misconception is that algorithms silently adapt; instead, the compiler enforces iterator requirements. Before calling an algorithm, verify its required category and match it to your container. The immediate question to ask yourself is: will the algorithm need to jump around or just scan sequentially? Algorithms and their iterator requirements means match algorithm requirements to an iterator category; random access is required for algorithms that jump around.. In practical terms, why some algorithms require random access iterators. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Algorithm needs
keyIdea.text: Match algorithm requirements to an iterator category; random access is required for algorithms that jump around.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Algorithm requirements
Algorithms that scan
std::find, std::for_each, std::count_if — these only need forward or input iterators because they examine elements sequentially.
They work with many containers and are flexible for streaming-style processing.
Algorithms that jump
std::sort requires random access iterators because it performs non-sequential access and indexing.
If your container doesn't provide random access, use a container-specific member algorithm like list::sort.
Example
std::sort(v.begin(), v.end()); // vector OK
Pitfall
std::sort(list.begin(), list.end()); // compile error — list is bidirectional
Key Takeaway

Always confirm the iterator category required by an algorithm and match it to your container.

screens.title: Common STL algorithms
screens.narratorSegment: STL offers many reusable algorithms that operate on ranges defined by iterators. std::find searches for the first occurrence of a value and returns an iterator to it or end if not found. std::for_each applies a function or lambda to every element in a range — it's convenient for side-effect work such as printing. std::transform maps an input range to an output range by applying a function to each element; the output range must have space allocated. std::count_if tallies elements that satisfy a predicate. A concrete flow: use std::find to locate a value, use std::for_each to log elements, use std::transform to build a new container of computed results, and use std::count_if to measure how many elements meet a criterion. Important practical notes: check that the output iterator for std::transform has sufficient space; when using std::for_each prefer lambdas to keep logic inline. A common misconception is that std::remove_if erases elements — it only reorders elements and returns a new logical end. Use erase with the returned iterator to physically remove elements. In practice, learning to combine these algorithms with lambdas dramatically reduces boilerplate loops and clarifies intent.

keyIdea.title: Useful algorithms
keyIdea.text: Use find, for_each, transform, and count_if to search, apply, map, and measure over iterator-defined ranges.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Common STL algorithms
std::find
Returns iterator to first matching element or end.
Use std::distance to compute the position when needed.
auto it = std::find(v.begin(), v.end(), value);
if (it != v.end()) {
  auto pos = std::distance(v.begin(), it);
}
std::for_each
Applies a function to each element for side effects.
std::for_each(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int n){ std::cout << n << " "; });
std::transform
Maps input range to output range using a function.
std::transform(in.begin(), in.end(), out.begin(), [](int n){ return n*n; });
std::count_if
Counts elements satisfying a predicate.
int c = std::count_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int n){ return n > 40; });
Common mistake

Remember std::remove_if only rearranges elements and returns a new logical end; you must call erase to shrink the container.

screens.title: Erase-remove idiom
screens.narratorSegment: The erase-remove idiom is a two-step pattern used to remove elements that satisfy a predicate from sequence containers like std::vector. std::remove_if reorders elements, moving those that do not match the predicate to the front of the range and returns an iterator to the new logical end. It does not change container size; it simply compacts the remaining items. To physically erase the unwanted tail, call container. erase(new_end, container. end()). This two-step process is necessary because algorithms like std::remove_if operate on ranges expressed by iterators and cannot call container-specific erase operations directly. A concrete example: to remove even numbers, call remove_if with a lambda checking n % 2 == 0, then erase from returned iterator to end. A common misconception is expecting remove_if to delete elements; forgetting erase leaves spurious values past the new logical end and does not reduce size. Another practical note: after erase, any iterators that pointed into the erased region are invalidated, so re-obtain iterators if you continue iterating. The erase-remove idiom is an idiomatic, efficient way to filter containers in idiomatic C++ code. Erase-remove idiom means use remove_if to compact, then erase the tail to actually remove elements and shrink the container.. In practical terms, how remove_if and erase work together to filter containers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Erase-remove idiom
Why two steps?
Algorithms like remove_if reorder elements but cannot resize the container. The container itself must perform erasure.
Example
auto new_end = std::remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int n){ return n % 2 == 0; });
v.erase(new_end, v.end());
Misconception
Calling remove_if alone will not shrink the container; it only returns a new logical end.
Iterator note
After erase, iterators into the erased range are invalid; obtain fresh iterators if continuing work.
Key Takeaway

Remember: remove_if compacts, erase removes. Use both to filter a container safely.

screens.title: Lambda functions with algorithms
screens.narratorSegment: Lambda functions are anonymous function objects that you can define inline when calling algorithms. They consist of a capture clause in square brackets, a parameter list, and a body. The capture clause controls how the lambda accesses variables from the surrounding scope. Capture by value copies the variable into the lambda; capture by reference allows the lambda to modify the original. For many algorithm situations, capturing by value is safe and avoids accidental modification, but when you need to update counters or accumulators outside the lambda you must capture by reference. A concrete example is using std::count_if with a threshold captured by value to test elements against a fixed limit. Another example uses std::for_each with a reference capture to increment a counter as elements meet a condition. A common pitfall is capturing a variable by value and expecting the outer variable to change; that will not happen. Also take care when capturing large objects by value — prefer references or const references when needed. Lambdas keep algorithm calls concise and expressive, and mastering capture semantics prevents subtle bugs in closures.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Lambda functions
Capture by value
[threshold] copies threshold into the lambda so the outer variable is not modified.
int threshold = 5;
int cnt = std::count_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [threshold](int n){ return n > threshold; });
Capture by reference
[&] or [&cnt] lets the lambda modify outer variables like counters.
int count_even = 0;
std::for_each(v.begin(), v.end(), [&count_even](int n){ if (n % 2 == 0) ++count_even; });
Pitfall
Capturing by value and expecting the outer variable to update will lead to surprising results. Choose capture semantics intentionally.
Key Takeaway

Lambdas make algorithms concise; always decide whether captures should be by value or by reference to avoid bugs.

screens.title: Iterator invalidation
screens.narratorSegment: Iterator invalidation occurs when an iterator no longer points to a valid element after a container operation such as insertion, erasure, or reallocation. Different containers have different invalidation rules. For std::vector, operations that grow the container beyond its capacity may reallocate memory, moving elements and invalidating all iterators. Even erase or insert at positions other than the end can invalidate iterators to elements after the change. std::list is more stable: erasing an element invalidates only iterators to that element while other iterators remain valid. A concrete example: if you keep an iterator returned by std::find and then call insert on the same vector, that stored iterator can become invalid, leading to undefined behavior when you use it. The recommended defensive approach is to re-obtain iterators after modifying containers or design algorithms that work with indices or fresh iterators. A common misconception is assuming iterators remain valid after push_back or insert; this depends on capacity and container type. The safety habit is to assume modification may invalidate iterators and code accordingly so that your program avoids undefined behavior and subtle bugs.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Iterator invalidation
Why iterators become invalid
Operations that reallocate or move elements may change addresses so stored iterators no longer refer to valid elements.

  • • std::vector: insert/erase can invalidate iterators after the operation.
  • • std::list: erasing an element invalidates only iterators to that element.
Concrete pitfall
Store an iterator from find, then insert into the same vector — the stored iterator may be invalid. Always re-obtain it after mutations.
Defensive rule
Assume modifications may invalidate iterators and write code to refresh them when needed.
Pro tip
When performance allows, work on copies or use indices where iterator invalidation is a concern.
Key Takeaway

Understand your container's invalidation rules and re-obtain iterators after operations that change storage.

screens.title: Filtering and transforming sensor readings
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the hands-on activity: filter sensor readings below a threshold and convert remaining Celsius values to Fahrenheit. Start by printing the original readings to confirm source data. To filter, use the erase-remove idiom: copy the original vector if you need to preserve it, call std::remove_if with a lambda that returns true when a reading is below the threshold, then call erase with the iterator returned by remove_if to physically shrink the vector. After filtering, prepare an output vector sized to the filtered container and call std::transform with a lambda that applies F = C * 9/5 + 32 to each element, writing the results into the output. Important practical notes: ensure the output vector has sufficient space before calling std::transform, and be mindful of iterator invalidation when you erase elements. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Filtering & Transforming
Starter code
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>

std::vector<double> celsius = {5.5,12.0,8.2,15.1,9.9,20.3,7.8,11.5};
double threshold = 10.0;

// Filter (erase-remove idiom)
auto filtered = celsius; // keep original
auto new_end = std::remove_if(filtered.begin(), filtered.end(), [threshold](double c){ return c < threshold; });
filtered.erase(new_end, filtered.end());

// Transform to Fahrenheit
std::vector<double> fahrenheit; fahrenheit.resize(filtered.size());
std::transform(filtered.begin(), filtered.end(), fahrenheit.begin(), [](double c){ return c * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0; });
Notes
  • • Copy original if you need it later.
  • • remove_if returns logical end; erase removes remaining elements.
  • • Ensure output vector is sized before transform.

Compose algorithms and lambdas to express filtering and mapping clearly and safely.

screens.title: Safe iterator and algorithm patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Writing safe iterator-based code means establishing a few habits. First, always validate ranges: a correct [begin, end) prevents range errors and empty-range surprises. Second, prefer copying or using fresh iterators when modifying a container inside a loop; re-obtain iterators after operations that can reallocate or move elements. Third, when combining algorithms, ensure each algorithm's iterator requirements are met—don't pass bidirectional iterators to functions that need random access. Fourth, pre-size output containers before calling algorithms like std::transform to avoid writing into uninitialized space. Fifth, prefer member functions when a container provides a more efficient or appropriate operation, for example using list::sort on std::list instead of std::sort. A concrete pattern is using erase-remove safely: compute new_end = remove_if(...), then container. erase(new_end, container. end()), and only then continue iterating with fresh begin/end. A common misconception is that generic algorithms will silently handle mismatched iterator capabilities; instead compilation will fail or behavior will be incorrect. These patterns reduce undefined behavior and make code easier to reason about—what is one small change you can make to an existing loop to use an algorithm instead? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on two interlocking parts of the STL: iterators and algorithms. Iterators act like generalized, safe pointers that let code traverse containers without knowing how the container stores data. Algorithms are generic functions that operate over iterator-defined ranges, following the common convention of including the first iterator but excluding the second—what we call the range from begin up to, but not including, end. You will learn how iterator categories determine what operations are available, why some algorithms require certain categories, and how lambda functions make algorithms concise and expressive. We'll work through examples with std::vector and std::list, demonstrate common algorithms such as std::sort, std::find, std::for_each, and std::transform, and show the important erase-remove idiom for filtering data. Along the way, you'll see practical pitfalls like iterator invalidation and how to avoid them. By the end of this chapter you will recognize the right iterator category, choose the correct algorithm for a task, and write compact, safe transformations using lambdas. Think about a container you use most often and how these tools will let you process its elements without writing container-specific loops.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to reason about iterators and use them confidently with STL algorithms. First, you will understand iterators as generalized pointers and the importance of the [begin, end) range convention. Second, you will be able to distinguish iterator categories — input, output, forward, bidirectional, and random access — and match them to algorithm requirements. Third, you'll use iterator-based algorithms such as std::sort, std::find, std::for_each, std::transform, std::count_if, and std::remove_if, applying lambda functions as concise predicates or operations. Finally, you'll master safety patterns like the erase-remove idiom and avoid iterator invalidation by re-obtaining iterators after modifying containers. Each objective focuses on both conceptual understanding and practical application so you can write idiomatic and safe STL code. Imagine filtering sensor readings with std::remove_if and transforming the remaining values with std::transform; these are the exact skills you'll practice. A quick verification milestone follows each objective so you can check your competency.

This continuation outlines practical checks and small skills to verify. You will practice reading and writing through iterators, using iterator arithmetic where supported, and understanding when to prefer container member algorithms like list::sort versus std::sort. You will also practice writing lambdas with different capture styles and see when capture by value or by reference is required. Finally, you will complete a hands-on activity: filter readings below a threshold and convert the remaining values using std::transform. These objectives emphasize doing as well as knowing. Each card includes a verification milestone so you can test competency: for example, sorting a vector with std::sort and confirming the order, or using the erase-remove idiom to remove elements and checking the container size afterward. These small checks help make conceptual learning immediately practical. Learning Objectives — continued means practice iterator read/write, algorithm selection by iterator needs, lambdas with capture, and the erase-remove idiom.. In practical terms, skills and practical checks. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An iterator is best understood as a generalized pointer that provides a uniform interface to traverse elements inside any STL container. It lets code use the same stepping and dereference operations across vectors, lists, sets, and other containers despite different underlying layouts. A container offers begin and end: begin returns an iterator to the first element, and end returns a sentinel positioned one past the last element. The half-open range [begin, end) is fundamental: it includes the element pointed to by begin and excludes the sentinel end. This convention simplifies loops and algorithms because an empty range has equal begin and end. A concrete example is iterating a vector with a traditional loop that increases the iterator until it equals end, dereferencing each iterator to access values. A common misconception is treating end as a valid element — dereferencing end is undefined. Another subtle point is that iterators hide container internals so your algorithm doesn't depend on contiguous memory or node structure. Key takeaways: treat iterators like pointers, always use [begin, end) to define ranges, and never dereference end. How might this change the way you write loops when switching from a raw array to an STL container?

Iterators support a small set of operations that depend on their category, but the most fundamental are dereference and increment. Dereferencing an iterator with the star operator gives access to the element; using pre-increment advances the iterator to the next position. With writable iterators you can assign through the dereference to change the container's element. For example, given a vector of integers you can loop using an iterator, multiply each value in place, and the container will be updated. A useful way to think about this is: iterators provide controlled access to elements without exposing container internals. One concrete example: replacing values by assigning *it = newValue inside a loop. A common misconception is treating iterators as indexes; while random access iterators support arithmetic like it + n, many iterators only allow ++ and cannot jump arbitrarily. When writing code, prefer range-based for loops when you only need read access, but use explicit iterators when algorithms require iterator types or when you need fine-grained control over traversal. Closing question: when would you prefer to write through an iterator instead of collecting results in a separate output container?

Iterator categories classify what operations an iterator supports and therefore what algorithms can use them. Input iterators allow single-pass reading with ++ and dereference for reading. Output iterators permit writing values once as you advance. Forward iterators can read and write multiple times while moving forward; they are multi-pass. Bidirectional iterators add the ability to move backward with --, which is necessary for containers like std::list. Random access iterators expose arithmetic such as it + n, it[n], and comparison operators so algorithms that jump around, like std::sort, can perform efficiently. A helpful way to remember this is as a capability ladder: each category adds more power. A concrete example: std::vector provides random access iterators, letting std::sort operate on it directly. std::list provides only bidirectional iterators and cannot be sorted with std::sort; instead use list::sort. A common misconception is expecting all containers to support random access operations; this will either fail to compile or be inefficient. When choosing an algorithm, check the minimum iterator category it requires. Which container you pick often determines which algorithms are available to you. Iterator categories means iterator categories add capabilities; match an algorithm's requirement to a container's iterator.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

STL algorithms are written generically, but many depend on the iterator category for correctness or performance. For example, std::sort requires random access iterators because it needs to jump to arbitrary positions and compare elements at non-sequential offsets; these operations use iterator arithmetic and indexing. Attempting to pass std::list iterators to std::sort will fail at compile time because std::list provides bidirectional iterators only. In contrast, std::find and std::for_each work with input or forward iterators because they only move forward and examine elements sequentially. The implication is practical: choose container types based on the algorithms you intend to use. If you need frequent random-access sorting and indexing, std::vector is a natural fit. If your data needs stable iterators when inserting and erasing in the middle, std::list offers stability but sacrifices random access. A common misconception is that algorithms silently adapt; instead, the compiler enforces iterator requirements. Before calling an algorithm, verify its required category and match it to your container. The immediate question to ask yourself is: will the algorithm need to jump around or just scan sequentially? STL offers many reusable algorithms that operate on ranges defined by iterators. std::find searches for the first occurrence of a value and returns an iterator to it or end if not found. std::for_each applies a function or lambda to every element in a range — it's convenient for side-effect work such as printing. std::transform maps an input range to an output range by applying a function to each element; the output range must have space allocated. std::count_if tallies elements that satisfy a predicate. A concrete flow: use std::find to locate a value, use std::for_each to log elements, use std::transform to build a new container of computed results, and use std::count_if to measure how many elements meet a criterion. Important practical notes: check that the output iterator for std::transform has sufficient space; when using std::for_each prefer lambdas to keep logic inline. A common misconception is that std::remove_if erases elements — it only reorders elements and returns a new logical end. Use erase with the returned iterator to physically remove elements. In practice, learning to combine these algorithms with lambdas dramatically reduces boilerplate loops and clarifies intent.

The erase-remove idiom is a two-step pattern used to remove elements that satisfy a predicate from sequence containers like std::vector. std::remove_if reorders elements, moving those that do not match the predicate to the front of the range and returns an iterator to the new logical end. It does not change container size; it simply compacts the remaining items. To physically erase the unwanted tail, call container. erase(new_end, container. end()). This two-step process is necessary because algorithms like std::remove_if operate on ranges expressed by iterators and cannot call container-specific erase operations directly. A concrete example: to remove even numbers, call remove_if with a lambda checking n % 2 == 0, then erase from returned iterator to end. Another practical note: after erase, any iterators that pointed into the erased region are invalidated, so re-obtain iterators if you continue iterating. Another example uses std::for_each with a reference capture to increment a counter as elements meet a condition. A common pitfall is capturing a variable by value and expecting the outer variable to change; that will not happen. Also take care when capturing large objects by value — prefer references or const references when needed. Lambdas keep algorithm calls concise and expressive, and mastering capture semantics prevents subtle bugs in closures.
